headlines.article_text: Stocks moving the most today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images A slate of artificial intelligence stocks surged on the heels of Jensen Huang's return to the helm of Nvidia, with CoreWeave and Micron Technology soaring on Monday. A rally in gold prices also lifted shares of mining stocks like Newmont and Gold Fields. Follow below as CNBC highlights the biggest stock moves of the day. 45 Min Ago Mining stocks rally alongside the price of gold and copper December gold futures rallied Monday Mining stocks rallied Monday alongside bullish moves in the price of gold, silver and copper. Gold futures climbed about 4%, silver by roughly 5% and copper added nearly 3%. Newmont Mining , AngloGold Ashanti , Coeur Mining and Gold Fields Ltd. all surged more than 7%, while Freeport McMoRan jumped almost 8%. — Scott Schnipper 47 Min Ago IP shares fall after its board approves spinoff In this photo illustration, the International Paper logo seen on a smartphone and on a computer screen. Pavlo Gonchar | SOPA Images | Lightrocket | Getty Images Shares of International Paper fell 4% after the packaging solutions company announced Monday that its board had approved the spinoff of its Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) packaging business into a publicly traded company, DS Smith. International Paper will remain an important shareholder, retaining a 19.9% stake. The company expects to complete the separation and distribution on Dec. 7, 2026, after the satisfaction of customary conditions and regulatory approvals are met. Additionally, the company announced its intention to delist from the London Stock Exchange after the completion of the separation. — Deena Zaidi 1 Hour Ago Artificial intelligence names are soaring as Huang returns to Nvidia A slate of stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade skyrocketed on Monday as Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. Dell Technologies and neocloud CoreWeave were last up about 22%, while data center power play Bloom Energy surged 19%. Photonics stock Lumentum popped 18%. Memory stocks also surged, with the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) gaining 19%. Rallies in SK Hynix and Micron Technology , both up around 20%, lifted the ETF. — Darla Mercado 1 Hour Ago Boeing shares rise after President Trump says he expects China to buy 250 more aircraft Shares of Boeing popped over 4% after President Donald Trump said on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " that he expects China to buy another 250 Boeing jets. BA News of the additional aircraft orders comes roughly six months after the May summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump. At the time, Trump said that China would purchase 200 Boeing jets , an agreement that Beijing confirmed . — Ananya Chetia 4 Hours Ago CoreWeave, Oracle surge on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang return Shares of CoreWeave and Oracle jumped 20% and 12%, respectively, following the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as Nvidia CEO. The companies, as well as neoclouds like Nebius and IREN , were among the hardest hit after Huang's resignation ignited fears about Nvidia's role in financing AI companies . The company, known as the "central bank of AI," had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Oracle lost 10% in the last month, while CoreWeave sank 13%. Nebius and IREN lost 37% and nearly 40%, respectively, during that time. Nebius rose 29% and IREN gained 27% on Monday. — Michelle Fox 4 Hours Ago Nvidia surges after reinstating Huang as CEO Shares of Nvidia surged 28% in premarket trading after the company reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO . Huang stepped down Nov. 12 amid an adultery scandal, sending the stock plummeting and igniting fears over the artificial intelligence trade. Nvidia is down 40.5% in the past month. — Michelle Fox 5 Hours Ago General Motors moves higher after report on Barra successor CEO and Chair of General Motors Mary Barra delivers a speech during the brand's annual technology event in New York on Oct. 21, 2026. Charly Triballeau | AFP | Getty Images Shares of General Motors added more than 2% following a Bloomberg report that said executive Sterling Anderson is being considered as a potential successor to CEO Mary Barra. The company's board wants the next leader to have an expertise in software and self-driving technology, Bloomberg said, citing people familiar with the board's thinking. Anderson came to GM in June 2025, leaving behind the self-driving vehicle technology startup he co-founded, Aurora Innovation. Prior to that he was the director of autopilot programs at Tesla. — Michelle Fox 6 Hours Ago Dollar General rises on upgrade A Dollar General store in Denver, Colorado, US, on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Chet Strange | Bloomberg | Getty Images Shares of Dollar General moved 2% higher on the back of an upgrade to overweight from neutral at Piper Sandler. Analyst Peter Keith said comparable sales growth and margin expansion should help the discount retailer reach a high-teens earnings-per-share compound annual growth rate over the next three years. Plus, the company's steady growth profile is appealing in an increasingly volatile market environment, he said. — Michelle Fox 6 Hours Ago LuxExperience pops after JPMorgan upgrade JPMorgan upgraded the luxury digital retailer to overweight from neutral on Monday, sending U.S.-listed shares up 6.6% in premarket trading. headlines.article_text: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $44B deal as AI supercharges cyberattacks Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CrowdStrike agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at $43.9 billion. In this article CRWD ZS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:05 04:05 Dan Ives: This is just the start of a golden age for cybersecurity Morning Call CrowdStrike plans to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal that combines two significant security businesses at a time when artificial intelligence is supercharging attacks. Shares of CrowdStrike dropped 10% on Monday, while Zscaler surged more than 15%. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028. Under the agreement, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share. CrowdStrike's acquisition pushes the Austin, Texas-based cyber vendor into the network security market and comes amid a massive year for cybersecurity deal-making in the wake of high-profile hacks like Hugging Face. "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." Recent outages affecting Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and JPMorgan Chase have sparked anxiety as businesses accelerate software patching and upgrades to aging systems in an effort to prevent bad actors from exploiting software vulnerabilities with AI. CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion. The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks. Last year, Google announced plans to acquire Wiz for $32 billion. In 2024 Cisco shelled about $28 billion for Splunk. Competitor Palo Alto Networks has also spent billions on several cyber and AI businesses, including startup Applied Compute and a $25 billion deal for CyberArk, which it closed earlier this year. Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan. CrowdStrike on Monday also reported better-than-expected fiscal third-quarter results , including earnings of 34 cents per share on $1.58 billion in revenue. That topped the 31 cents per share on $1.53 billion in revenue forecast by LSEG. Zscaler's fiscal first-quarter earnings , also released on Monday, likewise surpassed estimates. SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
headlines.summary: The states are seeking civil penalties and injunctions to stop Grok and X from creation and distribution of nonconsensual sexualized images.
headlines.article_text: SpaceX sued by 2 states over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue Elon Musk's SpaceX, alleging it harmed consumers and falsely marketed its Grok AI image generator as generally safe. Grok, which is integrated with social network X, has enabled users to generate and share explicit deepfakes based on real images of children and women who did not consent, research shows. The states' attorneys general are seeking civil penalties, fees and to make SpaceX put stricter guardrails in place. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty Images Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator. Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others. In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material. The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content. Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images. "This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation." In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors." At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products. SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California. In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction. When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content. SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions." The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company. Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance. State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms. In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.
